vignette:
She is 31, European, divorced, and works as a paramedic, a job she once described as the place where she feels most useful and most in control. Before the incident, she moves through her shifts with the steady focus that emergency work demands: checking equipment, reading rooms quickly, noticing what others miss, keeping her voice calm when the world around her is not. She has been used to blood, panic, broken bones, and grief. What she is not used to, and what changes her, is being on the receiving end of violence from police.

The traumatic event happens during an evening call that begins, in her mind, as routine and then becomes surreal and dangerous. She is responding to a chaotic scene with flashing lights, shouting, and too many bodies moving at once. She recalls trying to do her job, trying to reach a person who needs help, when police officers turn their attention toward her and her partner. The details come back to her in fragments: a hand gripping her arm too hard, the shock of being ordered to move when she is already complying, the humiliating escalation that follows when she tries to identify herself. She remembers the sudden, sharp fear of realizing that the uniforms and authority she has always associated with protection are now the source of threat. There is a sense of disbelief that lingers even as the event unfolds, as though her mind is refusing to accept what her body already knows.

Afterward, she is physically unharmed enough to go home, but she does not feel the same in her body. In the days that follow, she replays the scene again and again, especially the moment she was grabbed and the tone of command in the officers’ voices. She wakes with her heart racing, already tense before she opens her eyes. At work, she becomes hyperalert in a way that others notice before she does. A siren, a radio crackle, footsteps in a hallway can make her flinch. She scans every scene for exits, for hands, for badges, for any sign that someone might become aggressive. She says she is fine, but her body remains braced, as if another confrontation could start at any second.

She starts avoiding anything that reminds her of the event, though she cannot fully avoid the job that surrounds her with reminders. She delays looking at news reports involving police. She changes the channel when footage of arrests appears. She finds herself refusing certain calls when she can, especially those that might take her near large public disturbances or police activity. Even at home, she tries to keep distance from anything that might bring the memory forward. Yet the memory comes uninvited. A shout in the street, a strong male voice in a store, the sight of flashing red and blue lights reflected in a window can pull her back into the moment with startling force. In those moments she is not in her kitchen or on a sidewalk; she is back in the scene, flooded with the same fear and humiliation.

She also carries a deep mistrust that has spread beyond the original event. Before, she had a clear sense of how authority worked. Now she is suspicious in a way that feels exhausting and unfamiliar. She watches people’s hands and questions their intentions. She has trouble feeling safe, even with colleagues she knows well. At times she becomes irritable and sharp, especially when she feels cornered or dismissed. She says she is “short-fused now,” but the phrase does not quite capture the way she moves through the world with a constant readiness to defend herself. Sleep is poor, and when she does sleep, it is light and broken. She feels detached from friends and has pulled back socially, telling people she is busy or tired. Her divorce predated the trauma, but she now talks about the relationship with a flatness that suggests how much of her emotional energy is spent simply getting through the day.

As she tells her story over several sessions, it becomes clear that the worst part is not only what happened, but what it meant. She had built her identity around being helpful, steady, and professional. Being harmed by police while trying to help leaves her with a painful contradiction she cannot neatly resolve. She still shows up for work, still does her job, still moves toward emergencies when others are moving away. But she does so with a tighter jaw, a quicker startle, and the constant effort of holding herself together long enough to make it through another shift.
